activity_event_idempotency.backfill: one-time, in the same statement that creates the claim trigger and under a SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE lock on activity.events, so no event lands between them without a key; guarded on the trigger's presence, so later inits do not rescan activity.events. Existing duplicate rows are kept, and each key is given to its earliest occurrence

claim.held_key: honoured only while the event it names is stored: the BEFORE INSERT trigger then returns NULL, so the event row is skipped with no error and no RETURNING row, exactly like an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING that met its conflict. A key whose event is not stored is moved onto the new event
claim.occurrence_key: a row whose (occurred_at, idempotency_key) another subject's stored event already holds is handed to that key unclaimed (ON CONFLICT skips it, a plain INSERT raises), so no key is claimed for a row that is never stored

activity_event_idempotency.design_decision: activity.events is partitioned by occurred_at, so its own unique key must include occurred_at and cannot see a retry stamped a moment later or routed to another partition. This non-partitioned table holds one row per (subject_id, idempotency_key), claimed by a BEFORE INSERT trigger on activity.events, so a second insert of the same key is skipped whatever its occurred_at, including under concurrent inserts. The events table's UNIQUE (occurred_at, idempotency_key) is kept, additively, because writers name it as their ON CONFLICT target; subject-scoping it would be a coordinated breaking change, so the claim defers to it instead.

erasure.count: activity.erasures.idempotency_keys_deleted, a nullable BIGINT: the erasure procedure counts the subject's keys before it deletes the events, because the triggers delete them
erasure.event_release: activity_events_release_idempotency_key, AFTER DELETE on activity.events: deleting an event releases the key it holds, so deleting a subject's events removes their keys
erasure.subject_release: activity_user_subjects_release_idempotency_keys, AFTER DELETE on activity.user_subjects: removing the pseudonym link removes the subject's keys that name no stored event
erasure.summary: personal data keyed to subject_id, closed at the schema level: catalog-api's existing erasure transaction (delete events and impressions by subject, then the user_subjects link, under SET LOCAL groovemap.erasure = 'on') leaves no key row without naming this table

activity_event_idempotency.immutability: activity.reject_key_mutation(): UPDATE and DELETE of a key whose event is stored are rejected unless groovemap.erasure is on, as on activity.events; a key naming no stored event may be moved or removed

retention.procedure: run right after dropping an activity.events month partition, with the dropped partition's upper bound; it removes only keys older than the bound whose event is no longer stored and returns the count. Until then a retry under a dropped month's key is stored afresh, so the dedup window is the retention window

activity_event_idempotency.consumer_rollout: expand phase: catalog-api pins the revision containing this table, treats a skipped retry (no RETURNING row) as already recorded, and may record idempotency_keys_deleted in its erasure row; its erasure statements need no change. deployment's partition-drop runbook adds the purge call

catalog_item_supersession.design_decision: Declared exactly as design ADR 0009's 2026-09-25 amendment ('Superseded catalog items and native-id merge') names it, so catalog-api can code its merge steps 4-7 to the record. The resolution is a function rather than a view because it is defined for any native id, including ids with no catalog_items row (activity.impressions.item_id and the outcome endpoint record ids verbatim); a view keyed on catalog_items would drop those or push the COALESCE into every reader. catalog_item_moves carries from_item_id and to_item_id beside the amendment's columns, so a revert moves a row back only while it still points at to_item_id.

ledger.erasure: personal data keyed to user_id: the erasure procedure deletes a user's rows and export includes them; deleting the users row cascades

catalog_item_supersession.note: A superseded catalog item keeps its catalog_items row; a supersession row records its current survivor, closed by valid_to on revert. Resolution is always one hop: when a survivor is itself superseded, the writer closes the old row and opens one to the new survivor naming the compressing row as via_id. graph.catalog_item excludes currently superseded items. This repository declares the shape only; catalog-api writes every row inside the ADR 0014 transactions and enforces that both items share a kind.

resolution.meaning: the survivor_id of native_id's current supersession row, or native_id itself when there is none; one probe of the current-survivor index

supersessions.decision_ref: the matching decision row for edition_promotion, the admin_audit_log entry for catalog_reattachment; not a foreign key

compatibility.destructive_changes: require a new major contract and an explicit migration
compatibility.rollback: every destructive migration requires a tested rollback or restore procedure

extraction_history_source.data: no default and no backfill: rows written before the column existed keep source NULL, meaning the extractor was not recorded
extraction_history_source.consumer_rollout: expand phase: catalog-api pins the revision containing this column before it writes or reads source

columns.loader_extraction_latch.generation: BIGINT NULL (legacy rows retain NULL until the loader cutover)
columns.loader_extraction_latch.purge_vetoed: TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}' (entity types whose stale-row purge this extraction vetoed; rows written before the column read as none)

extraction_latch.design_decision: Named public.loader_extraction_latch and shaped with a loader discriminator so the loader family can share one relation, matching discogs-sql-loader's tableinator/extraction_latch.py startup probe: it checks public.loader_extraction_latch against information_schema, requires the loader column (REQUIRED_COLUMNS) along with the other non-key columns at their exact information_schema types, and scopes every statement to loader = 'discogs' (its own _key_columns() and ON CONFLICT (loader, version)). It verifies via pg_constraint that a PRIMARY KEY or UNIQUE constraint spans exactly (loader, version); a bare unique index is declined by design. Declaring the loader column and the composite primary key here up front means the loader's repin needs no statement changes. musicbrainz-sql-loader will write loader = 'musicbrainz' rows into the same relation when it adopts the pattern.
extraction_latch.note: A durable, per-(loader, extraction) latch recording which of a loader's entity types have signalled one extraction's `extraction_complete`, and whether that loader's post-import derived-relation refresh has completed for it (`refreshed_at`). Written before the triggering delivery is acked, so a restart resumes signal collection instead of losing it. Mirrors graphinator's Neo4j-side latch. This repository writes no row; discogs-sql-loader is the writer today, and musicbrainz-sql-loader may write its own (loader, version) rows into the same relation when it adopts the same pattern.

cursor.meaning: The latest accepted extraction for each loader. Serialize first-signal generation assignment with SELECT FOR UPDATE on this row. A worker locks it again just before commit and may publish only if its generation and version are still current.

derived_refresh_job.owner: database-schema declares DDL; each loader owns only its discriminator's rows
derived_refresh_job.semantics: The future loader commits the final signal and pending job before acknowledging its delivery. It scans due and expired jobs at startup and periodically, claims transactionally with row locking, and fences on both lease token/epoch and the per-loader cursor at the refresh transaction's commit. Refresh, latch stamp, and completed state commit atomically. A failure rolls back or schedules bounded retry; a superseded generation cannot stamp refreshed_at. No delivery may be acknowledged while its sole refresh obligation is in process memory.
derived_refresh_job.rollout: Schema first. Existing latch rows have NULL generation and remain readable by the current inline writer; the loader cutover must reconcile any unfinished legacy latch before acknowledging a terminal signal under the new protocol. Neither relation schedules work until a loader adopts it. Reverting the loader to inline behavior is safe while retaining these additive objects.
derived_refresh_job.failure_visibility: The loader must expose pending age, current and last completed versions, attempt count, lease expiry, retry due, sanitized last failure, and superseded count; the schema stores these facts but does not report health itself.

link_matches_event.link_added: discogs_id_before IS NULL and discogs_id_after IS NOT NULL
link_matches_event.link_removed: discogs_id_before IS NOT NULL and discogs_id_after IS NULL

identity_link_events.design_decision: One store for the Identity Ledger's dated link changes, from both the one-time full-export backfill and live loads. provider_aliases and catalog_item_supersessions stamp now() at write time and a supersession's cause is a closed set, so neither can date a link change. dated_from keeps the two provenances apart: a backfilled event reads 'dated from the MusicBrainz full export' because about 9% of its dates belong to older links MusicBrainz replaced, while a load event is dated by its own transaction. discogs_id_before and discogs_id_after are BIGINT, the type of the musicbrainz.*.discogs_*_id columns. entity_kind takes the values provider_aliases uses for MusicBrainz rows. decision_ref is a bare UUID naming the backfill run's admin_audit_log entry and is NULL for a load row. No user data is stored.

idempotence_key.meaning: a rerun of the same backfill or load inserts the same keys, so INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes it a no-op

indexes: idx_identity_link_events_entity_event_at ON identity_link_events (provider, entity_kind, external_id, event_at)
identity_link_events.consumer_rollout: expand phase: catalog-api and musicbrainz-sql-loader pin the revision containing this table before they write or read it

identity_ledger_precompute.design_decision: catalog-api's Identity Ledger works list and density routes computed every release item's event history per request (71.5 s p95 for the default works list at 50% scale, against a 2 s budget), and no index helps because each statement aggregates the whole history before it filters. Four tables hold what those statements compute, and a fifth rolls the works list up per UTC day (gm-database-schema-9dcd), all maintained off the request path by one function. They were materialized views until gm-database-schema-xen5: REFRESH recomputes all history whether or not anything changed, and CONCURRENTLY diffs every row, so a materialized view cannot cost less than its history (45 s on lux to produce 4 rows). The definitions remain catalog-api's route SQL with the filters lifted out, as its prototype composed them (scripts/ledger_scale.py, _view_statements, catalog-api 6d744e2); identity_ledger_verify() and the integration suite pin the tables to them. They are declared after the graph statements because the capture triggers and the refresh reach graph.derived_from.
identity_ledger_precompute.populate: every table is created empty, so applying the schema never runs the whole history inline; identity_ledger_refresh_state holds no row until the first refresh commits, and that row, not the tables' emptiness, answers 'refreshed yet?', because a catalog with no events is empty too; reapplying the schema never empties a table

refresh.freshness: all four tables commit together in the refresh's one transaction; a change committed after the refresh drained the log can show in part, and stays in the log, so the next refresh is exact and nothing is lost; freshness is bounded by catalog-api's refresh trigger, since this repository never calls the function
refresh.locking: the refresh writes rows under ordinary row locks, so readers never block and keep the previous rows until it commits, the first build included; it takes the advisory lock hashtext('groovemap:identity-ledger-refresh') that catalog-api already holds, so refreshes run one at a time
refresh.privilege: SECURITY INVOKER: the caller needs SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on IDENTITY_LEDGER_REFRESH_GRANTS and SELECT on the six sources. catalog-api connects as the login that owns public, like every service (deployment .env.example), and EXECUTE defaults to PUBLIC, so no grant is declared. The capture functions are SECURITY DEFINER, so a writer of a source needs no grant on the log
refresh.returns: refreshed_at, the instant the refresh started; the whole refresh and the state upsert run in the caller's one transaction
refresh.maintenance: per item: statement-level AFTER triggers on the six sources append each change to identity_ledger_changes in the writer's transaction, and signed link and supersession counts to identity_ledger_density_changes; a refresh drains both and recomputes only the dirty items, their editions, and those editions' works. The first refresh, a TRUNCATE of a source, a change to an item's id or kind, identity_ledger_request_rebuild(), and a refresh finding over 10% of the catalog dirty (and over 100,000 items) rebuild from the base tables instead. A refresh with no change writes only the state row. A refresh refuses to run while any capture trigger is missing or disabled
refresh.verify: public.identity_ledger_verify() RETURNS TABLE (relation text, missing bigint, unexpected bigint, pending_changes bigint) runs the full recompute against the tables in one statement and writes nothing, at the cost of one full recompute; the ledger equals a full recompute when every row is 0, 0, 0
refresh.rebuild: public.identity_ledger_request_rebuild() RETURNS void makes the next refresh a full rebuild

refresh_state.meaning: one row (singleton BOOLEAN PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT true CHECK (singleton)), upserted by each refresh with its start instant, duration, and the caller's watermark (JSONB, NULL when the caller names none); empty until the first refresh

identity_ledger_edition_events.meaning: every non-mint event of a release item, per edition (the item resolved one hop), instant and type, with its count; both sides of a supersession count

identity_ledger_edition_parents.meaning: every work parent of every evented edition: the Discogs master through graph.derived_from and the release group through musicbrainz.releases, each through its current alias, resolved one hop

indexes: idx_identity_ledger_work_summary_page ON public.identity_ledger_work_summary (event, last_event DESC, work_id)
identity_ledger_work_summary.meaning: one row per work with event = 'any' (every event type), plus one per work and event type; repaired means reattached, promoted, or reverted. The 'any' sentinel, not NULL, keeps (event, work_id) a unique key

identity_ledger_work_summary_day.meaning: the works list's rollup per UTC day, for windows of full days. One row per work, event filter ('any', an event type, or the pseudo filter 'repaired' for reattached, promoted or reverted), day and prev_day; editions counts the work's editions with an event of that filter on that day, and prev_day is that edition's previous day with an event of the same filter, '-infinity' for its first. WINDOW RULE for full UTC days [a, b]: evented_editions = sum(editions) over event = F, day in [a, b] and prev_day < a, which counts an edition once at its first day in the window; repaired_editions = the same over event = 'repaired' when F = 'any', editions itself when F is a repair type, and 0 otherwise; first_event and last_event = min(first_event) and max(last_event) over every row of event F with day in [a, b]. Summing editions over days without the prev_day condition counts an edition once per day it has events

identity_ledger_density.meaning: events per UTC month, type and provenance for each of release, master, artist and label, as catalog-api's density statement counts them

identity_ledger_precompute.consumer_rollout: expand phase first: catalog-api drops the relkind = 'm' filter from its two freshness statements and also requires the state row to exist, which holds on both shapes, and only then does this revision apply. The upgrade applies with loaders running: a guarded transaction drops the views and the state row, and the first refresh after it rebuilds from the base tables. Rollback is IDENTITY_LEDGER_ROLLBACK_STATEMENTS followed by the previous release's schema apply and one refresh; both ledger shapes hold derived rows only, so no history is at risk. See docs/architecture.md
identity_ledger_precompute.shape_change: The four relations were materialized views through v0.6.3. They keep their names, columns, column types, column order, and unique and read indexes, and a reader's SELECT is unchanged. What changes: pg_class.relkind is 'r', not 'm'; relispopulated is always true; reading before the first refresh returns no rows instead of raising SQLSTATE 55000; so 'not refreshed yet' is the absence of the state row. A reader that filters relkind = 'm' finds no relation and answers 'not refreshed yet' until it stops filtering, which fails safe on the admin routes alone.

stores.identity_ledger_item_mints: each item's mint as last computed, which a later refresh subtracts from density; the ledger's largest relation; no consumer reads it
stores.identity_ledger_item_events: each item's alias-derived events as last computed, likewise; no consumer reads it
stores.identity_ledger_changes: what changed since the last refresh; appended by the triggers, drained by the refresh; no consumer reads it
stores.identity_ledger_density_changes: signed density deltas waiting for a refresh; no consumer reads it

bootstrap.note: A one-off fill deriving every loader-written table from the catalog documents, using the same definitions those relations published as views before they were tables. It is NOT authoritative: the owner recorded against each relation writes it and supersedes this fill on its first pass. It exists so an environment can be populated once, before a loader has run, so a read rewrite is not blocked on the dual-write. Nothing calls it; applying the schema declares it and writes no row. Each relation is emptied and refilled in one transaction, so re-running converges in both directions and a row no document justifies is removed. It reports a row count per relation. graph.artist_member_of is derived from the relations above it rather than from a document, so the fill shares one body with graph.refresh_artist_member_of and the two cannot disagree; graph.vertex_degree is derived the same way, from the ten path relations, and shares its body with graph.refresh_vertex_degree. Those two relations are the ones with a named refresh owner, which the fill does not supersede. One known divergence: a company with no Discogs id is keyed on its name case-folded, and this fill folds with SQL lower where the loader applies Python casefold, so a handful of characters key differently and the loader's row is the correct one. graph.track_credited_on and graph.track_by_artist (gm-database-schema-ug3v) fill from a document's tracklist and each track's sub_tracks, the same shape discogs-sql-loader's own track-level derivation reads; the loader's row is authoritative on any disagreement, exactly as it is for the other twenty-nine.

counter_properties.note: graphinator writes these onto the Neo4j node of the same name. The relational contract publishes them through a view joining its storage relation to its counter relation; the counter relation is unique on the join column, so the planner removes the join for a query that reads no counter. A count reads zero where the loader has not computed one; first_year stays null. graph.release_degree remains a separate relation because its live half is a pair of lateral counts no unique key makes removable.

explore_function.declared_as: graph.explore_traversal(from_kind "char", from_key text, hops int DEFAULT 2, row_limit int DEFAULT 100) RETURNS TABLE (id text, name text, type text, path_names text[], rel_types text[], dist int)
explore_function.note: The bounded breadth-first replacement for catalog-api's get_explore_traversal Cypher. It walks the same undirected BY, ON, IS, ALIAS_OF, MEMBER_OF, and DERIVED_FROM surface as graph.find_shortest_path, recording one parent pointer per discovered vertex and walking those pointers back to project path_names and rel_types. It returns only Artist, Label, Genre, and Style discoveries; Release and Master vertices remain valid intermediate path nodes. Breadth-first discovery is non-decreasing by distance, so the walk stops once row_limit qualifying vertices have been discovered rather than materialising the full three-hop traversal before limiting. The row limit is mandatory: NULL is rejected because the spike measured the unbounded three-hop translation at 21.4 seconds and the bounded procedural form at roughly 15 ms locally, about 1,400 times faster. hops is clamped to [1, 3], preserving catalog-api's existing Explore contract. The function reuses the session-local graph_path_seen relation as its seen set and frontier, creates no persistent relation, reads graph.artist_member_of for the cross-provenance MEMBER_OF edge, and does not read graph.vertex_degree because a one-sided breadth-first walk has no search side to choose.

free_text_keys.credit_key_hash: graph.text_key over the name's length, a colon, the name, and the role
free_text_keys.hash: sha256 of the value's UTF-8 bytes
free_text_keys.migration: A guarded transaction per relation builds the unique index and any hash index, then drops the primary key and the indexes that stored the raw column. A database already on the v0.6.1 two-hash credit keys has a second guarded transaction per credit relation, which builds the combined key, drops the old one, renames it, and drops the relation's person_name hash index. Both run with the loaders stopped and neither rewrites the table.
free_text_keys.note: PostgreSQL refuses a btree entry over 2704 bytes after compression, and these columns are free text with no bound, so a credit past the limit could not be stored. Each relation keeps its key columns and its whole value; a UNIQUE index over graph.text_key enforces the key in place of a primary key, and a hash index keeps = on the column where a consumer reads by it. credited_on and track_credited_on have none, and key both free-text columns through graph.credit_key. No column is added, so a writer's column list is unchanged. A target-less ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING fires on the unique index; an ON CONFLICT naming the columns does not infer it, and none of the loaders uses one.

key_columns.note: Key columns are not all text. Discogs vertex and edge keys (artist_id, label_id, master_id, release_id, medium_id, company_id, sublabel_id, and the genre, style, person, and media-family names) are text: the four Discogs vertex views publish data_id::text and the loader-written tables are declared text from the start, which retires the graph.artist.artist_key, graph.label.label_key, graph.master.master_key, and graph.release.release_key restatements. The exceptions are recorded under types and are the types the relations actually declare: uuid for the identifiers of the application-owned relations and for every MusicBrainz mbid, bigint for track ordinals and MusicBrainz relationship ids, and "char" for graph.vertex_degree.kind. graph.collected.release_id and graph.wants.release_id also publish data_id::text, so every Discogs graph key is text and a join against graph.release.release_id needs no cast; schema init converges an existing database by dropping and recreating those two views when the column still reads as another type.

types.text: every other key column of every loader-written table, and the key column of the Discogs vertex views (graph.artist.artist_id, graph.label.label_id, graph.master.master_id, graph.release.release_id) and of graph.collected.release_id, graph.wants.release_id, graph.sublabel_of, graph.part_of, graph.in_family, and graph.release_degree

member_of_union.note: Neo4j holds a Discogs band membership and a MusicBrainz member-of-band assertion in one MEMBER_OF relationship space, so shortestPath traverses both without knowing which is which. On the relational side they are two relations in two key spaces: graph.member_of is Discogs-only and keyed on Discogs artist ids, while the MusicBrainz half lives in musicbrainz.relationships keyed on MBIDs and reaches a Discogs id only through musicbrainz.artists.discogs_artist_id. Spike gm-database-schema-gkt.1 measured 22,577 Discogs rows against 36,189 MusicBrainz ones, so 61.6% of that edge class is MusicBrainz provenance and a traversal over graph.member_of alone returns different paths from the Cypher it replaces. This relation resolves the crossing once at build time, with source in the key so the same membership asserted by both providers is two rows rather than a collision. It binds no property-graph label: a second artist-to-artist edge label overlapping member_of would double-count every Discogs membership in a pattern that matched both. The refresh is truncate-and-insert, so it converges in both directions and reports a row count per provenance; discogs-sql-loader calls it on the extraction_complete latch it already handles, the same latch the counter relations are recomputed on.

neo4j_only.decision: Recorded as Neo4j-only, not published relationally. No relational reader of any of these is known today, and publishing a relation of about 5.0M rows (the distinct-pairs count from Postgres; lux has no HAS_STYLE edges yet) with no reader and no writer would add load cost for nothing. Publishing them later is additive; would_publish_as names the shape a later bead would add.

artist_properties.label: artist
artist_properties.would_publish_as: graph.artist_stats keyed on artist_id, joined into graph.artist_vertex beside graph.artist_degree, with discogs-sql-loader as writer
artist_properties.note: graph_schema.counter_properties.labels.artist.properties stays [degree] on purpose: check-contracts.py proves each listed property is a column of graph.artist_vertex, and these three are not.

HAS_STYLE.cardinality: one per label and style, no cap
HAS_STYLE.observed_count: about 5.0M distinct (label, style) pairs, counted from Postgres; lux has no HAS_STYLE edges yet
HAS_STYLE.effect_on_path_surface: None. HAS_STYLE is outside the relationship types graph.find_shortest_path walks, so that function, graph_path rels and edge_relations are unchanged.
HAS_STYLE.would_publish_as: a loader-written graph.label_style table keyed (label_id, style_name) carrying release_count, derived from graph.on_label and graph.in_style

ExtractionCompletion.stats_version.note: A persisted property of the Neo4j ExtractionCompletion node. It is not a column of this schema and is not published relationally.

MaintenanceCheckpoint.run_key.note: A persisted property of the Neo4j MaintenanceCheckpoint node; it is not graph.extraction_latch, which keys on (loader, extraction) and is unchanged.

graph_schema.note: Twenty relations are loader-written tables replacing a view that computed the same rows on every read, seven more hold the counters, degrees, and genre aggregates the graph enrichers compute today, one more is the cross-provenance MEMBER_OF union recorded under graph_schema.member_of_union, one more is the per-vertex degree recorded under graph_schema.vertex_degree, two more (graph.track_credited_on and graph.track_by_artist) are the track-level credits and performers that never had a view, which makes thirty-one tables, and the remaining thirty-seven relations are read-only views over tables declared elsewhere in this contract. This repository declares every one of them and writes rows into none: the owner named against each relation does that, so an empty table on a fresh database is the expected state rather than a fault.

path_function.declared_as: graph.find_shortest_path(from_kind "char", from_key text, to_kind "char", to_key text, max_depth int DEFAULT 6) RETURNS TABLE (found boolean, depth int, nodes text[], rels text[])
path_function.nodes: One entry per vertex from the source to the target, each the pair kind:key. The key half is what the Cypher returns per node, coalesce(node.id, node.name), so a Genre or a Style is its name and every other vertex is its Discogs id; the kind half is the one-byte discriminator graph.vertex_degree is keyed on. The pair is what makes the answer unambiguous, because an Artist and a Release can hold the same numeric key and a bare id could not say which vertex a hop went through.
path_function.note: The one Cypher call this schema cannot express as a view: shortestPath over BY|ON|IS|ALIAS_OF|MEMBER_OF|DERIVED_FROM, ported from spike gm-database-schema-gkt.1's prototype. It is a vertex-at-a-time bidirectional search. It expands one vertex of the smaller-summed-degree frontier at a time in ascending graph.vertex_degree order, probes each expanded vertex against the whole of the opposite seen set, and returns at first touch. First touch is exact because the probe compares against the opposite SEEN set rather than the opposite FRONTIER: with df and db the depths each side is complete to, a touch at depth b <= db from a frontier vertex at df witnesses a walk of length df + 1 + b, the invariant says no path of length <= df + db exists, and the two bounds meet at df + db + 1. A side's completed depth therefore advances only when its level finishes, the expansion writes rows for the side being expanded and no other so the opposite seen set is frozen for the level, and the distance is read off the recorded depths rather than asserted, so a mistake in that argument shows up as a disagreement with Neo4j instead of as a silently wrong answer. It writes no graph relation and no persistent relation of any kind: its only state is one session-scoped seen set. A search that finds nothing returns one row with found false and the other three columns null, where the Cypher returns no row at all. The depth clamp is catalog-api's MIN_PATH_DEPTH, MAX_PATH_DEPTH and DEFAULT_PATH_DEPTH unchanged; spike gm-database-schema-gkt.1 recommended a cap of 4 instead, because at cap 10 a distance-6 pair costs 4.1 s on its cloud machine against 10.5 ms at cap 4 and nothing in the catalog is answerable at 5 or 6 inside the request budget. The owner chose 10 anyway, for exact parity with the Cypher this replaces, and accepts seconds beyond depth 4 for it; lowering the default is a change to the callers' contract rather than to this function.
path_function.rels: One entry per hop, so one shorter than nodes, each the Neo4j relationship type of that hop: BY, ON, IS, ALIAS_OF, MEMBER_OF, or DERIVED_FROM. It is the type and never the provenance. graph.artist_member_of carries source, but Neo4j holds both provenances in one relationship space and reports one type, and projecting source would cost a heap fetch on every backward hop because the reverse index (group_artist_id, member_artist_id) does not cover it.

seen_set.created_by: graph.find_shortest_path, on its first call in a session
seen_set.note: One request-scoped relation and no second frontier relation: the frontier is side = s AND depth = d over the relation being written anyway, which the secondary index makes an index-only scan of the level. The spike measured a separate queue costing a second heap insert, a second index insert and a sequence nextval for every vertex discovered, and dropping it cut the worst measured case by about two fifths. It is TEMPORARY rather than UNLOGGED because two concurrent searches against one unlogged table would corrupt each other, and ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS because the spike's per-call TRUNCATE was about 4 ms of a 5.2 ms floor. It is not an hstore and not an array: a PL/pgSQL variable is passed into a SQL statement by value and re-serialised on every statement, so those representations are faster below a few thousand vertices and do not finish at all above a hundred thousand. A consumer never names this relation; it is recorded so that a session holding one after a search is understood as expected state rather than as a leak.
seen_set.shape: TEMPORARY table, ON COMMIT DELETE ROWS

vertex_degree.note: One bigint per vertex of the path traversal surface, holding its undirected degree. It decides expansion order only - which side of a bidirectional search to expand next, and which vertex of that side's frontier to expand first - and changes no answer. Spike gm-database-schema-gkt.1 measured the distance-5 variance falling from 1,774 ms to 334 ms with it and unchanged answers; it does not help distance 6 and made it slightly worse, so it is a variance reducer rather than a fix. It is 97 MB at catalog scale against the 1,649 MB spike gm-database-schema-9c8.3 priced for a dense adjacency copy. kind is a one-byte discriminator rather than a prefix on the key because the pathfinder's node identity is the pair and an equality on a concatenated token cannot use the edge tables' text indexes. Only a vertex carrying an edge has a row; a lookup that misses reads as degree zero. A membership both provenances assert counts twice, because graph.artist_member_of carries source in its key and an expansion of that vertex really does scan two rows. It binds no property-graph label: it is an ordering heuristic for the path functions, not a property of any Neo4j node. The refresh is truncate-and-insert, so it converges in both directions and reports a row count per vertex kind; discogs-sql-loader calls it on the extraction_complete latch it already handles, the same latch the counter relations are recomputed on and after graph.refresh_artist_member_of, which writes one of the ten relations it sums.

view_evolution.allowed: appending a column to the end of an existing view
view_evolution.engine_enforcement: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW fails the statement outright rather than replacing the view
forbidden: renaming a view or a view column
view_evolution.migration: expand, migrate consumers, then contract, with a coordinated DROP ... CASCADE
view_evolution.shape_change: A relation that becomes a loader-written table is replaced by a guarded migration that drops the view only when one is still there, in the same pass that creates the table. The published column names survive the change; the key columns are retyped from character varying to text, which psycopg returns identically.

master_search.backfill: CALL public.master_search_backfill(batch_pages integer DEFAULT 1000, first_page bigint DEFAULT 0), run once by the operator outside a transaction block; the initializer never runs it. Each batch takes SHARE on public.master_search (never a lock on masters beyond a read's ACCESS SHARE), so readers never block and a load's trigger waits at most one batch; first_page resumes from its last progress notice; its heap pass upserts, rewriting a row only when its vector or year differs, so it also repairs stale rows; rerunning it is harmless; its SQL runs in step functions with a pinned search_path, and PUBLIC has no EXECUTE on it or them

columns.master_id: VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, equal to masters.data_id
columns.year: TEXT, NULL when the document has no year

master_search.consumer_rollout: expand phase: catalog-api ranks, year-filters and decade-facets masters by master_search only after master_search_drift() reports no missing rows on that database; until then it keeps reading masters.data through idx_masters_fts, which this change leaves in place
master_search.design_decision: Master search and the masters half of the decade facet computed to_tsvector over masters.data for every match and read each match's heap row of whole documents (lux: 2.6M masters, 2.4 GB of heap at about nine a page; 'love' 71,692 matches, 69,224 buffers for the ranked branch, 0.97 per match). A side table built by the same generator as release_search holds the vector and the year, so a ranking or a facet reads a narrow row per match and reads masters only for the rows that survive its LIMIT; on a lux-shaped 2.6M-row sample 'love' falls from 1.05 to 0.38 buffers per match (2.8x) and from 6.6 s to 0.18 s cold, with the same 40 results in the same order; a side table rather than columns on masters for the reasons release_search gives (gm-database-schema-nu0c)
master_search.drift: public.master_search_drift() RETURNS TABLE (missing bigint, orphaned bigint, stale bigint); missing and orphaned read keys only, stale recomputes every vector and year together and so reads every document
master_search.maintenance: triggers on public.masters keep it current, so no loader changes: an insert or delete is captured once per statement, an update only when it sets data_id or data (so the loaders' updated_at refresh and identity backfill pay nothing), and a truncate empties it; a capture writes a row only when its vector or year changed; the capture functions are SECURITY DEFINER, so a role that writes masters needs no grant on master_search; each refuses to run on any table but public.masters, and PUBLIC has no EXECUTE on them
master_search.rollback: the statements in MASTER_SEARCH_ROLLBACK_STATEMENTS, in order; they touch no masters row and nothing of release_search
master_search.vector: to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(data->>'title', '')) of the master's data, the expression idx_masters_fts indexes, for every master and no other row
master_search.year: data->>'year' of the master's data verbatim, as text: catalog-api's (year)::int filter and its '^[0-9]{4}$' decade test apply to it unchanged, and no document value can make a capture fail

musicbrainz_delete_reconciliation.note: musicbrainz.relationships and musicbrainz.external_links were declared with created_at only, unlike every other MusicBrainz entity table. The additive updated_at column closes the gap: the loader refreshes it on every upsert and reconciles deletes by removing rows where updated_at < run start, the same purge_stale_rows shape discogs-sql-loader already runs against the Discogs entity tables' own updated_at. DDL ownership is database-schema alone, so this column is declared here rather than carried as a startup ALTER in the loader.

key.conflict_target: ON CONFLICT (musicbrainz.relationship_key(source_mbid, target_mbid, source_entity_type, target_entity_type, relationship_type, begin_date, end_date, attributes))

retired.was: UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT over the same eight columns
retired.guard: dropped only when relationships_key exists and is unique, valid and ready; otherwise the statement keeps the constraint and raises a notice
retired.never_recreated: neither the CREATE TABLE nor the five-column migration declares it, so applying the schema again does not bring it back
retired.breaking_for: an ON CONFLICT (<eight columns>) target, which then fails with: there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification

rollout_order.step: database-schema adds musicbrainz.relationship_key and the unique index musicbrainz.relationships_key beside the constraint
musicbrainz-sql-loader moves its conflict target to the expression
rollout_order.requires: musicbrainz-sql-loader v0.6.0 or later, deployed and running
no writer still names the eight columns as its conflict target

rollout_order.step: MusicBrainz is enabled and the first load runs
rollout_order.requires: the contract phase has been applied

musicbrainz_relationship_key.note: The hash key is the old constraint's rule except that attributes is hashed as jsonb text: key order does not matter, but a number keeps its written scale, so 1 and 1.0 are two keys where jsonb equality calls them one. With the constraint retired they are two rows. A NULL value is one key and is distinct from an empty string and from jsonb null. MusicBrainz attributes are strings and arrays of strings, so none is known to hit the scale case. No index leads with source_mbid after the drop: a source_mbid lookup is answered by idx_mb_rels_endpoint_source (source_entity_type, target_entity_type, source_mbid) through PostgreSQL 18's B-tree skip scan.
musicbrainz_relationship_key.rollback: Restore the constraint with ALTER TABLE musicbrainz.relationships ADD CONSTRAINT relationships_natural_key UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT (source_mbid, target_mbid, source_entity_type, target_entity_type, relationship_type, begin_date, end_date, attributes); it builds a unique index over the table, so it takes a write lock for the build and fails if the table holds two rows that the jsonb comparison calls equal (the 1 and 1.0 case). Applying the schema does not restore it. A writer that names the eight columns may run again only after that.

release_search.attributes: gm-database-schema-1sle: catalog-api's facet and filter inputs, each exactly the expression it evaluates over releases today, so its genre, decade and media facets and its year, genre, media and country filters can read release_search instead of detoasting releases.data per match; nothing is typed or cleaned, so a clause answers the same for every row and no value can make a capture trigger fail
release_search.backfill: CALL public.release_search_backfill(batch_pages integer DEFAULT 1000, first_page bigint DEFAULT 0), run once by the operator outside a transaction block; the initializer never runs it. Each batch takes SHARE on public.release_search (never a lock on releases beyond a read's ACCESS SHARE), so readers never block and a load's trigger waits at most one batch; first_page resumes from its last progress notice; its heap pass upserts, rewriting a row only when one of its values differs, so it fills columns added to a populated table and repairs stale rows; rerunning it is harmless; its SQL runs in step functions with a pinned search_path, and PUBLIC has no EXECUTE on it or them

columns.country: TEXT, data->>'country' of the release, exactly as catalog-api's country filter (= ANY) reads it
columns.genres: JSONB, data->'genres' of the release, exactly as catalog-api's genre filter (?|) and facet (jsonb_array_elements_text) read it
columns.media_families: JSONB, media->'families' of the release, exactly as catalog-api's media filter (?|) and facet (jsonb_array_elements_text) read it
columns.media_mediums: JSONB, jsonb_path_query_array(media, '$.items[*].medium[*]'): NULL exactly when media is NULL (catalog-api's media IS NULL), and media_mediums ? m exactly when jsonb_path_exists(media, '$.items[*] ? (@.medium == $m)', ...)
columns.release_id: VARCHAR PRIMARY KEY, equal to releases.data_id
columns.year: TEXT, data->>'year' of the release, exactly as catalog-api's year filter (::int) and decade facet (~ '^[0-9]{4}$') read it; TEXT like master_search.year

release_search.consumer_rollout: expand phase: catalog-api ranks by title_tsv only after release_search_drift() reports no missing rows on that database; until then it keeps ranking by idx_releases_fts, which this change leaves in place; catalog-api moves its facets and filtered release branches onto the attribute columns only after the backfill that follows this upgrade and a drift of (0, 0, 0); until then it reads releases as today
release_search.design_decision: Ranking a common title term computed to_tsvector for every match, detoasting the whole releases.data document per match (lux: 'love' 497k matches, about 4.7 buffers each, 16.6 s first run). A side table holds the vector so a ranking reads a row of about 86 bytes per match and reads releases only for the rows that survive its LIMIT. A side table rather than a column on releases: a stored generated column rewrites the table under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and a nullable column filled in batches writes a new version of all 19.6M rows into every index on releases, while the side table is created empty and filled without writing to releases (gm-database-schema-fi4a)
release_search.drift: public.release_search_drift() RETURNS TABLE (missing bigint, orphaned bigint, stale bigint); missing and orphaned read keys only, stale recomputes every carried column and so reads every document
release_search.maintenance: triggers on public.releases keep it current, so no loader changes: an insert or delete is captured once per statement, an update that sets data_id or data rewrites every column, an update that changes media (WHEN OLD.media IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.media, via release_search_capture_update_media) rewrites media_families and media_mediums only and never reads data, and a truncate empties it; so the loaders' updated_at refresh and identity backfills pay nothing; the capture functions are SECURITY DEFINER, so a role that writes releases needs no grant on release_search; each refuses to run on any table but public.releases, and PUBLIC has no EXECUTE on them
release_search.rollback: move catalog-api's readers back to releases first; then the statements in RELEASE_SEARCH_ROLLBACK_STATEMENTS, in order (they also drop the media trigger and its function); they touch no releases row
release_search.upgrade: from v0.11.0's (release_id, title_tsv): each attribute column is added by ALTER TABLE public.release_search ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS, nullable with no default (a catalog change under ACCESS EXCLUSIVE on release_search only, about 1 ms each on a populated table; skipped, taking no lock, once the column exists), and the five triggers are recreated together under SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE on releases (about 4-6 ms); the columns are NULL until CALL public.release_search_backfill() fills them
release_search.vector: to_tsvector('english', COALESCE(data->>'title', '')) of the release's data, the expression idx_releases_fts indexes, for every release and no other row

reload_seen_lists.design_decision: A reload proved a row still upstream by rewriting it for updated_at: discogs-sql-loader's hash gate touched every unchanged row and musicbrainz-sql-loader's upserts rewrite every conflict, because the stale-row purge deletes what updated_at says the extraction did not reach (measured on a lux-shaped releases sample: 230 us and 7.8 KB of WAL a row, 0 HOT; about 150 GB and 75 minutes for lux's 19.6M releases). A seen list records the same fact without the rewrite: the loader appends the row's key, in the transaction that would have touched the row, to a narrow, unlogged, index-free list (14-18 us and under 2 bytes of WAL a row), and the purge deletes a row only when it is older than the extraction AND not in the list. One design for both loaders, by operator decision 2026-11-04 (gm-database-schema-uw6d, gm-discogs-sql-loader-g77f, gm-musicbrainz-sql-loader-3osm).

loader_seen.discogs_artists.seen_key: TEXT NOT NULL, the row's data_id

loader_seen.discogs_labels.seen_key: TEXT NOT NULL, the row's data_id

loader_seen.discogs_masters.seen_key: TEXT NOT NULL, the row's data_id

loader_seen.discogs_releases.seen_key: TEXT NOT NULL, the row's data_id

loader_seen.musicbrainz_relationships.seen_key: BIGINT NOT NULL, loader_seen.hash_key(musicbrainz.relationship_key(source_mbid, target_mbid, source_entity_type, target_entity_type, relationship_type, begin_date, end_date, attributes))

loader_seen.musicbrainz_external_links.seen_key: BIGINT NOT NULL, loader_seen.hash_key(musicbrainz.external_link_key(mbid, entity_type, service_name, url))

list_columns.seen_at: TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), the appending transaction's start, as updated_at = NOW() was

reload_seen_lists.storage: UNLOGGED, no index, no key, autovacuum_vacuum_insert_threshold = -1; append-only between restarts, emptied only by loader_seen.start; duplicates are expected and harmless

registry.storage: UNLOGGED, so crash recovery empties it together with the lists it vouches for
registry.intact: a list is intact for an extraction when its registry row exists and opened_at <= started_at - 15 minutes (the clock margin between the extractor's started_at and the database's now())

functions.loader_seen.start(p_loader text, p_data_: TRUNCATE the one list and stamp its registry row with now(), in the caller's transaction; raises 22023 for an unknown list
functions.loader_seen.status(p_loader text, p_data: seen_keys counts distinct keys appended at or after p_started_at; one scan of the list; raises 22023 for an unknown list
functions.loader_seen.<list>_stale(p_started_at ti: the purge set: rows of the reconciled table with updated_at < p_started_at AND no key in the list since p_started_at; returns data_id text for Discogs lists and id bigint for MusicBrainz lists; raises 55000 when the list is not intact
functions.loader_seen.<list>_shadow(p_started_at t: for a shadow reload, which still touches: touch_purge is the old purge set (updated_at < p_started_at), seen_purge what the seen purge deletes once the touch is gone (not in the list); any refreshed_not_seen blocks the switch
functions.loader_seen.hash_key(key bytea) RETURNS: the first 8 bytes of a key hash; IMMUTABLE STRICT; a collision only keeps a stale row one more month
functions.musicbrainz.external_link_key(mbid uuid,: SHA-256 of the link's unique key, length-prefixed as musicbrainz.relationship_key is; IMMUTABLE

loader_obligations: append every row a batch processes (inserted, changed, unchanged, and each sighting of a MusicBrainz child row) to its list in the batch's own transaction, on every write path

before a purge: skip it, as for a dead-letter veto, when loader_seen.intact is false, or when status.seen_keys is below the guard fraction of the extractor's record_counts for that type (Discogs); keep PURGE_MAX_DELETE_FRACTION on the stale set
purge from loader_seen.<list>_stale only; delete graph rows and entity rows by the returned ids, not by updated_at
call loader_seen.start for the list when the extraction settles for it (purged, vetoed or skipped), in the purge's transaction when it purges
never TRUNCATE or DELETE from a list directly

consumer_rollout.step: database-schema adds loader_seen; the initializer starts every list once, when it creates it
each loader appends, keeps the touch and the updated_at purge, and logs loader_seen.<list>_shadow at every purge for one full reload

with operator approval, once a shadow reload reports refreshed_not_seen = 0 and touch_purge = seen_purge (or every difference explained): stop touching unchanged rows and purge from loader_seen.<list>_stale
drop idx_<table>_updated_at if no reader remains; a separate database-schema change

reload_seen_lists.rollback: a loader switches back to the touch and the updated_at purge by configuration; the first purge after switching back still sees every unchanged row as stale, so it must be a reload with the touch on, not a purge of the reload that ran without it. The schema's own rollback is SEEN_LIST_ROLLBACK_STATEMENTS: DROP SCHEMA loader_seen CASCADE and drop musicbrainz.external_link_key; no other relation reads them

retired_relations.consumer_rollout: contract phase of expand, migrate consumers, then contract: catalog-api stopped writing and reading both tables (gm-catalog-api-gz4r) and operations-console reads queue and service-health history from VictoriaMetrics, so the drop lands only after a catalog-api release containing that removal is deployed
retired_relations.data: historical rows are not migrated; VictoriaMetrics holds the same series at finer resolution for its retention window (ADR 0018)
